query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of molybdenum into the boride layer on hot-dip aluminum-plating components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A boride-based coating on structural components used in hot-dip aluminum plating without Mo incorporation.
generation.intervention: Integrate a small, controlled amount of molybdenum (e.g., via doping during the boriding process) to produce a Mo-enriched boride coating.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at typical plating temperatures (around 660°C) under service conditions encountered in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of Mo-enriched boride phases that promote the development of a more stable, passivating surface oxide (or boride) layer.
generation.mechanism: Molybdenum is known to improve passivation capacity and mitigate localized dissolution by forming more protective surface phases. In the boride phase, Mo incorporation reduces the vulnerability of the coating to aggressive molten aluminum, thereby slowing the corrosion process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated boride-coated components, the Mo-doped boride coating is expected to show a measurable decrease in corrosion indicators (e.g., lower corrosion current density and reduced weight loss or surface degradation) when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components with no added molybdenum.
generation.boundary: The improved performance is expected under standard hot-dip plating temperatures (approximately 660°C) and typical molten aluminum exposure durations; extreme mechanical stresses or chemical modifications of the aluminum bath may affect the outcome.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of corrosion resistance improvement is uncertain without targeted experimental data; the optimal Mo concentration and long-term stability under cyclic thermal conditions require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-coated specimens: one set with the standard boride coating and the other with a specifically Mo-doped boride coating. Subject both sets to identical immersion in molten aluminum (maintained around 660°C) for a fixed period. Post exposure, assess the specimens using weight-loss measurements, surface morphology analysis (e.g., SEM), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to quantify corrosion behavior.
measurements: Corrosion current density via electrochemical impedance measurements
Surface phase characterization (e.g., XRD, SEM/EDS) to confirm Mo incorporation and protective phase formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped specimens do not show a statistically significant decrease (beyond experimental error) in corrosion indicators (such as weight loss or corrosion current) compared to the undoped baseline, then the hypothesis that Mo addition improves corrosion resistance under molten aluminum conditions will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It was found that, by reducing the Mn concentration (to 5 at.% Mn), the CoCrFeMnNi alloy acquires higher yield strength values after annealing at 1117 K (from 387 to 477 MPa) due to the grain refinement effect (from 4.4 to 2.61 µm) []. Mn also shows a rapid evaporation effect during melting processes; hence, in our study, this element was replaced by Mo, which could improve the resistance to high temperatures []. Co–Cr–Mo alloy is widely used for manufacturing of vanes and gas turbines due to its excellent fatigue behavior and wear resistance [,,,]. In such alloys, molybdenum has a beneficial effect on passivation capacity, contributing to the formation of a protective surface layer that allows pitting corrosion to be limited [,]. Studies were conducted to estimate the effects on the microstructure and properties of alloys with different Mo contents [,,]. Such alloys have been designed for the manufacture of furnace casings and chemical tanks used in high-temperature and corrosion conditions [], for components used in the geothermal industry [,], or to obtain high-performance coatings [].
